items.title: The guessing machine
items.brief:
Picture-only sentence game. 0–4 s: many small picture tiles (cups of tea, coffee mugs,
water glasses, bowls of amahewu — tea cups most numerous) stream from the left into a simple
phone-shaped machine. 4–8 s: a half-sentence picture appears (a sunrise + a person + a cup
outline with a question mark). 8–11 s: the machine "thinks" (bubble pulses) and outputs the
most common tile — a teacup — with a confident bounce. 11–14 s: beside it, a learner figure holds
a different drink (amahewu); a small question mark appears between them. 14–16 s: fade back to
the start. No text.

items.title: Good photo, bad photo
items.brief:
Phone camera view of a leaf with holes. 0–3 s: dark, blurry, far away, sun flaring in
the lens. 3–6 s: the photographer turns so the sun (north, top of sky) is behind her — flare
gone. 6–9 s: phone moves close; leaf fills the frame. 9–11 s: a finger taps the leaf — it snaps
sharp. 11–13 s: a flat hand slides in beside the leaf for size; a tick appears. 13–14 s: hold.

items.title: A voice can be copied
items.brief:
0–4 s: a young man records a short voice note; a sound-wave shape leaves his phone.
4–8 s: the wave flies into a shadowy box that stamps out an identical wave. 8–12 s: the copied
wave arrives on his mother's phone from an unknown number with a coin and airtime icon beside it.
12–16 s: she lowers the phone, taps a saved contact with her son's face — the real son answers,
surprised; both shake heads. 16–18 s: a small padlock and a heart (code word) appear. No text.

items.title: Climb the Check Ladder
items.brief:
A farmer with a phone climbs the five-rung ladder from A-P07-ART. As she reaches each
rung (every 2.5 s), its small picture lights up: own garden with sun in the north → circular
arrow → seed packet and label → two people talking → one small row planted. At the top she
smiles and plants the row. Loop.

items.title: The sun is in the north (for "does it make sense here?")
items.brief:
Optional, for rung ① of the Check Ladder: "AI often answers with northern seasons.
Here the sun is in the north, and winter is June–July." Play once, no narration over it.

items.title: Look at the soil
items.brief:
Optional clip for "AI can't see your soil" — people observe soil with their own eyes
and hands. Show on a tablet to groups while they discuss what only people can do.

items.title: What the farm record shows
items.brief:
Optional, before reading an AI-written report: "A report is only as true as your
records. If the record says 12 bunches, the report can't say 50."

items.title: Learning together under a tree
items.brief:

a small community garden: a gogo, an older man in a hat, two young women, a young man. One
phone is shared between the gogo and a young woman; the young woman points at the screen, the
gogo laughs. The others lean in. A poster on a fence behind (plain shapes, no text). Midday
light, sun high in the north; soft shade. Leave the left third calm (Paper-coloured sky and wall)
for the slide title.

items.title: Our class and phone agreement
items.headline: Learn together, phones too
items.labels:
1. Phones silent, not away
2. Share the turn
3. Ask before photos
4. Private stays private
items.layout:
Headline top band; art 45%; labels as numbered callouts; a 20% blank panel with
ruled lines for the class's own rules (marker on paper, or a sheet taped on the banner).
items.teach_it:
```
A-P01  Our class and phone agreement            (≈ 8 min)
1. GROUPS: agree one rule that helps us learn together. 2 min.
2. Reporters say it; Recorder writes/draws it in the blank panel.
3. POINT ①: phones silent, not away — we use them in class.
4. POINT ②: one phone, many people — everyone gets a turn.
5. POINT ③: ask before you photograph a person (POPIA consent).
6. POINT ④: no ID, PIN or bank details typed today.
7. ASK: Can we all live with these? Thumbs up.
KEY: We share phones, we share turns, we protect each other.
```

items.title: AI is a guessing machine
items.headline: AI is a fast guesser
items.labels:
1. Learned from lots
2. Guesses what's next
3. Sure, but wrong
4. Knows what you show
items.layout: Headline top; art 60% flowing left to right; labels under the art in the callout band.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P02  AI is a guessing machine                  (≈ 20 min with the role-play)
1. PLAY: "Finish my sentence" — 3 starts, room shouts, tally the answers.
2. Put on the AI sign. Answer with the most common word, every time.
3. Ask the machine about a coughing goat — answer fast, sure, and unsafe.
4. Ask it when to plant maize — answer "April" (northern seasons).
5. Take the sign off: "Now I'm me again."
6. POINT ①→④ and say each label.
7. ASK: What doesn't it know about your farm?
KEY: AI is a very fast guesser. Very good is not always right.
```

items.title: Where you already meet AI
items.headline: AI is already here
items.labels:
1. Keyboard guesses words
2. Voice typing
3. Chat helper
4. Camera search
5. Translate
6. Garden app helper
items.layout: Headline top; phone centre with islands around; labels in a 2 × 3 grid at the foot.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P03  Where you already meet AI                 (≈ 12 min)
1. SAY: You've probably used AI this week. Let's find it.
2. GROUPS with a phone: find 3 places AI is on your phone.
3. EVERYONE: type "Good m…" and watch the keyboard guess ①.
4. GROUPS: sort the picture cards — used / not used.
5. Reporters name one each; tick the island on the poster.
6. ASK: Which one surprised you?
KEY: You already use AI — keyboard, mic, camera, chat.
```

items.title: Save your data
items.headline: Make your data last
items.labels:
1. Auto-download off
2. Standard photos
3. Data saver on
4. Updates on Wi-Fi
5. Voice, not video
items.layout: Headline top; the pot centre; five callouts in a ring; labels in the band below.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P04  Save your data                            (≈ 20 min)
1. ASK: What did you spend on data last week? Tell your neighbour.
2. Connect the group phone to the course Wi-Fi.
3. ① WhatsApp › Settings › Storage and data › Media auto-download › mobile data: none.
4. ② Photo upload quality › Standard.
5. ③ Phone Settings › search "data saver" › on.
6. ④ Play Store › auto-update on Wi-Fi only.
7. ⑤ Habit: voice notes use less data than video.
KEY: Learners tap it themselves. Menus differ — use Settings search.
```

items.title: The Question Hand
items.headline: Ask with your whole hand
items.labels:
1. Who I am
2. What I have
3. What I want
4. How to answer
5. Ask again
items.layout: Headline top; the hand fills 60%; labels as callouts beside each finger (large, 64 pt).
items.teach_it:
```
A-P05  The Question Hand                         (≈ 15 min + practice)
1. AI sign on. A learner asks one word: "Spinach?" Read B-00 — long, useless.
2. Sign off. Hold up your hand: "A good question has five fingers."
3. POINT ①–⑤ with an example: farmer near Bergville · spinach bed with holes ·
   stop it · 3 short steps in isiZulu · ask again.
4. AI sign on. Ask the full question. Read B-01 — short, useful.
5. ASK: Which answer helps more? Why?
6. PAIRS: say the five fingers in your own language.
KEY: Tell it who you are and what you have. The first answer is a draft.
```

items.title: Ask with your voice and a photo
items.headline: Say it. Show it.
items.labels:
1. Light behind you
2. Close up
3. Hold still
4. One thing
5. Show the size
6. Speak, then read
items.layout: Headline top; art split 25% voice / 35% photo; callouts beside; labels band.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P06  Ask with your voice and a photo           (≈ 7 min + stations)
1. ENERGISER: Broken Telephone — a farm sentence whispered round the circle.
2. SHOW: keyboard mic ⑥. Speak a question. Read what it wrote.
3. PAIRS: English, then first language. Fix mistakes.
4. SHOW two photos: dark and blurry vs clear. ASK: which can AI understand?
5. POINT ①–⑤. Add: both sides of a sick leaf, and the whole plant.
6. Ask before a person is in your photo.
KEY: Clear photo, better answer. A photo answer is still a guess — check it.
```

items.title: The Check Ladder
items.headline: Check before you trust
items.labels:
1. Makes sense here?
2. Ask again
3. Second source
4. Ask a person
5. Try it small
items.layout: Headline top; ladder rising left to right across 60%; labels next to each rung.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P07  The Check Ladder                          (≈ 8 min + Find the mistakes)
1. AI sign on: "Plant cabbage 5 cm apart." ASK: Would you do it? How did you know?
2. ASK: In the village, how do you check a rumour?
3. POINT ①→⑤ bottom to top; a learner says each rung in their language.
4. SAY: How high you climb depends on how bad a mistake would be (A-P08).
5. GROUPS: Find the mistakes — 4 B-cards; circle, colour, who to ask.
6. Reporters share one mistake each.
KEY: Makes sense? · ask again · second source · ask a person · try small.
```

items.title: Green · Orange · Red questions
items.headline: How bad if it's wrong?
items.labels:
1. Green: try small
2. Orange: check again
3. Red: danger
4. Red? Ask a person
items.layout: Headline top; three panels 60%; labels to the right of each panel.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P08  Green · Orange · Red                       (≈ 10 min)
1. POINT ① green: ideas, recipes, names, writing help — try it small.
2. POINT ② orange: planting dates, spacing, pests, prices — second source.
3. POINT ③ red: sprays and poisons, medicine, animal health, loans, grants,
   SASSA, contracts, land — ④ always a person. Never AI alone.
4. GROUPS: sort T-01…T-12 onto the three sheets. 6 min.
5. ASK groups: "What's the worst that could happen?"
KEY: The label is the law. Red questions go to a person.
```

items.title: Keep it private
items.headline: Your phone is your wallet
items.labels:
1. ID number
2. Bank card, PIN
3. Codes (OTPs)
4. Grant details
5. Children's faces
6. Where you are
items.layout:
Headline top; wallet 55%; "Never share" as a small Ochre tag above the six labels.
(The tag is 2 more words — total stays ≤ 25.)
items.teach_it:
```
A-P09  Keep it private                            (≈ 20 min with the sort)
1. ASK: What's in your wallet you'd never give a stranger?
2. SAY: Your phone is a wallet now.
3. GROUPS: sort the H-cards — fine / trusted face to face / never. 10 min.
4. POINT ①–⑥: never share with strangers or AI.
5. SAY (POPIA): the law protects your information; you can ask what an
   organisation holds and complain to the Information Regulator.
6. SAY: AI apps may keep what you type. Ask about spinach, not your bank.
KEY: Codes and PINs: never, to anyone.
```

items.title: Stop · Check · Ask
items.headline: Stop · Check · Ask
items.labels:
1. Don't click, pay, send
2. Call back, known number
3. Ask someone you trust
items.layout: Headline top; three panels 50%; warning-icon strip 15%; labels under the panels.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P10  Stop · Check · Ask                          (≈ 5 min + scam cards)
1. PLAY the fake voice note (Day 0 recording). ASK: What would you do?
2. POINT ①: STOP — scammers rush you.
3. POINT ②: CHECK — call back on the number you already have.
4. POINT ③: ASK — family, mentor, bank at the branch, SASSA office, police.
5. POINT the warning strip: hurry · secret · money/airtime/code · too good ·
   a link · pay a fee for a job, grant or loan.
6. GROUPS: sort S-01…S-10 — scam / real / not sure. 15 min.
KEY: Hurry + money or code = scam until proven real.
```

items.title: Fake voices, fake videos
items.headline: Voices and videos can lie
items.labels:
1. Voices can be copied
2. Too good? Too scary?
3. Call back yourself
4. Family code word
items.layout: Headline top; art in three panels 60%; labels in the band.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P11  Fake voices, fake videos                   (≈ 15 min)
1. SAY: AI can copy a voice from a short voice note, and make a video of a
   famous person saying things they never said.
2. ASK: How can you tell? Collect answers.
3. POINT ①–④.
4. SAY: Check the message, not the picture. Money, secrets or codes = stop.
5. PAIRS: role-play a family member "in trouble"; the other asks the code question.
6. SAY: agree the code word face to face. Never write it down or post it.
KEY: Call back on the number you know. Use a family code word.
```

items.title: AI drafts, you own it
items.headline: AI drafts. You own it.
items.labels:
1. Facts true?
2. Sounds like me?
3. Nothing private?
4. Would I sign it?
items.layout: Headline top; art 60%; four checks as a checklist band with tick boxes.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P12  AI drafts, you own it                      (≈ 8 min + practical)
1. ENERGISER: Human or Machine? — read D-00, stand/sit.
2. POINT ①–④: the four checks before you send.
3. SAY: CVs, funding requests, reports carry YOUR name. Never send what isn't true.
4. GROUPS: draft with AI (or use a D-sheet), then red-pen it.
5. [APP] till slip: check total, item, shop against the paper. The slip wins.
6. Two groups read their fixed version aloud.
KEY: AI drafts, you own it — every fact, every word.
```

items.title: What AI can't do
items.headline: Only people can do this
items.labels:
1. Feel your soil
2. Measure the rain
3. Elders' knowledge
4. Your mentor
5. Our languages — double-check
items.layout: Headline top; scene 60% with the small dark phone near the centre; labels in the band.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P13  What AI can't do                          (≈ 15 min)
1. SAY: Hands up if AI can do it, down if it can't.
2. ASK: see your soil? replace a soil test or scale? know your rain?
   know today's market price? know your gogo's knowledge? replace your mentor?
   sign for you?  — give the one-line answer each time.
3. POINT ①–④.
4. GROUPS: agree one thing only people can do; Recorder adds it beside the poster.
5. POINT ⑤: AI is weaker in isiZulu and Sesotho — double-check (Day 2 S4).
KEY: AI can't see your soil or feel the rain. People, land and elders first.
```

items.title: My AI plan
items.headline: Use it to think. Ask to decide.
items.labels:
1. Use AI for
2. Always ask a person
3. My data rule
4. My safety step
5. I will teach
items.layout:
Headline top (two short lines); art 55%; labels match the K-06 plan sheet line by
line, so learners can copy the shape.
items.teach_it:
```
A-P14  My AI plan                                 (≈ 15 min)
1. Hand out K-06. Point to ①–⑤ — the plan has the same five parts.
2. Learners fill it alone — words or drawings. 8 min.
3. REMIND: never write your family code word.
4. PAIRS: tell your plan; partner asks "What will you do first?"
5. Invite 2–3 volunteers to say one line to the room.
KEY: Use AI to think; ask a person to decide.
```

items.title: Our class agreement
items.headline: How we learn together
items.labels:
1. Our agreement (above the lines)
2. Sign here (small, beside a row of 30 empty thumb-print circles at the bottom)
items.layout:
Headline top; art band 35%; 12 ruled lines with a pale Leaf tint for writing;
30 thumb-print circles along the bottom edge.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: "What do we need from each other so everybody can learn?"
2. Write their words — not yours. Hand the marker to a learner.
3. Make sure these are there: phones silent · one voice at a time · right to pass · no laughing
   at anyone · everyone does the practicals · on time · what's personal stays here · respect
   the land.
4. Everyone signs or thumb-prints a circle.
KEY: If we forget, anyone can point to this poster.

items.title: Earth care · People care · Fair share
items.headline: Three ways to care
items.labels:
1. Earth care — soil, water, life
2. People care — family first
3. Fair share — give back the extra
4. All three together (centre)
items.layout:
Headline top; Venn fills 60%; labels outside each circle with a leader line.
Question strip: *"Which one do you already do?"*
items.teach_it:
1. Tell the story of Gogo Thandi and her neighbour (day-1.md S1).
2. ASK: who cared for soil? for people? who shared?
3. Point ① ② ③. One sentence each.
4. GROUPS: draw one thing you already do for each circle (8 min).
5. Reporters: one circle each.
KEY: Earth care, people care, fair share — together, not one at a time.

items.title: Two gardens
items.headline: Which garden will feed you in a drought?
items.labels:
1. Soil always covered
2. Many plants together
3. Water slowed and kept
4. Nothing wasted
items.layout:
Headline top; split art 60% (left slightly desaturated); numbered callouts ①–④ on
the right side only; question strip: *"What did your grandmother do?"*
items.teach_it:
1. Cover the right half. GROUPS: what will this garden look like in a drought? (3 min)
2. Reveal the right half. ASK: what is different?
3. Water-pour demo: bare brick vs mulched brick.
4. SAY: agroecology = farming with nature; permaculture = designing with nature.
5. Point ①–④.
KEY: Bare soil loses water and soil. Covered soil keeps both.

items.title: Six garden principles
items.headline: Six ways to garden with nature
items.labels:
1. Watch first
2. Catch and keep
3. Many helpers
4. Nothing is waste
5. Start small
6. Use the edges
items.layout:
Headline; 6-icon grid 70%; each label directly under its icon; blank flipchart
beside the poster for the magazine hunt.
items.teach_it:
1. For each icon: point, say the principle, ASK for one local example (2 min each).
2. GROUPS: magazine hunt — glue pictures under the six symbols (20 min).
3. Gallery walk; each Reporter explains one surprising match.
KEY: Watch first · catch and keep · many helpers · nothing is waste · start small · use the edges.

items.title: Read your land
items.headline: Read your land before you dig
items.labels:
1. Sun in the north
2. Shade to the south
3. Where water runs
4. Cold wind
5. Zones 0 1 2 3 4 5 (small numbers on the bands)
items.layout:
Landscape; headline top-left; art 75%; a legend column on the right with the five
colour ribbons used in the site walk (yellow sun, blue water, red wind).
items.teach_it:
1. Cardboard house in the sun: where is the shadow? (south) In winter? (longer)
2. SAY: plant vegetables north of the house.
3. GROUPS: site walk with yellow / red / blue ribbons (20 min).
4. Point to the zones: what you use every day goes by the door.
5. GROUPS: draw the venue land from above.
KEY: Watch first. Sun in the north. Every-day things closest to the door.

items.title: Build an A-frame
items.headline: Find the level line
items.labels:
1. Two legs, 2 m
2. Crossbar
3. String and stone
4. Mark · flip · mark
5. Middle = level
6. Peg and move
items.layout: Headline; big frame 45%; 3-step strip 20%; walking scene 15%.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: how do we find a line where water stands still?
2. Point ①–③ while groups build (20 min, one frame per group).
3. Calibrate: mark · flip · mark · middle (show once, every group does it).
4. Day 2: one foot on the peg, swing the other until the string hits the middle; peg; move.
KEY: Water on a level line stops and soaks in. Always calibrate.

items.title: Slow · Spread · Sink · Store
items.headline: Make the rain walk, not run
items.labels:
1. Slow it
2. Spread it
3. Sink it
4. Store it
5. Soil is the biggest tank
6. Greywater to trees, not leaves
items.layout:
Landscape; four bands across the top; flow art 70%; question strip: *"What is
the biggest tank on your land?"*
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: where did last summer's storm water go?
2. Tray demo: bare vs stones + grass (each group pours).
3. Walk the poster from roof to soil: ① ② ③ ④.
4. GROUPS: mark two water catches on every garden map.
KEY: Slow · spread · sink · store. Cover the soil — it is your biggest tank.

zu.headline: Yenza imvula ihambe, ingagijimi
zu.question: Yiliphi ithange elikhulu kunawo wonke endaweni yakho?

items.title: How much rain from your roof?
items.headline: 1 mm on 1 m² = 1 litre
items.labels:
1. Length × width = m²
2. × rain (mm) × 0.8
3. = litres caught
4. First rain goes out
5. Lid on
6. Overflow to the garden
items.layout:
Headline as a big equation; three bands (rule 25% · house 35% · tank 30%); a
blank white box (A4 size) where the facilitator writes the venue's own sum in marker.
items.teach_it:
1. Show the 1 ℓ bottle: 1 mm on 1 m² = 1 litre.
2. A 20 mm storm on 1 m² = one 20 ℓ bucket.
3. GROUPS: measure the venue roof on the ground.
4. Worked example: 10 × 6 = 60 m² · × 20 mm × 0.8 = 960 ℓ ≈ 48 buckets.
5. Counters method for anyone who prefers: one bottle top = 1 m² = 1 bucket.
6. Tank parts: gutter, first-flush, lid, tap, overflow.
KEY: Roof area × rain × 0.8 = the water you can catch.

items.title: A swale on the level line
items.headline: Catch the rain on the slope
items.labels:
1. Ditch on the level line
2. Soil below (mound)
3. Water soaks in
4. Plant the mound
5. Safe spillway
items.layout:
Headline; cross-section 60%; inset 20% top-right; question strip: *"Where at home
does water run away?"*
items.teach_it:
1. Safety: points down, nobody behind a pick, drink water, swap every 10 min.
2. Point ①–⑤.
3. GROUPS: mark the contour (everyone places the frame once), dig ditch above pegs, soil below.
4. Test with two 2 ℓ bottles: does water spread or run?
5. Mulch the mound.
KEY: Ditch on the level, soil below, safe spillway. Not on steep slopes.

items.title: Soil is alive
items.headline: Feed the soil, the soil feeds the plant
items.labels:
1. Squeeze
2. Jar
3. Smell and look
4. Count worms
5. Sand · Loam · Clay
6. 10+ worms = healthy
items.layout:
Headline; cut-away 55%; 4 test panels in a row 30%; question strip: *"What does
your soil need?"* (answer on the back: organic matter).
items.teach_it:
1. Two handfuls: alive vs dead soil — how do you know?
2. SAY: one handful of healthy soil holds more life than there are people in SA.
3. GROUPS: four tests, 7 min each (squeeze · jar · smell · worms + tin soak test).
4. Reporters: "Our soil is ___, it needs ___."
KEY: Sandy or clay — the answer is organic matter. Worms are free workers.

items.title: Build a compost heap
items.headline: Waste into food
items.labels:
1. Green (food)
2. Brown (bread) ×2–3
3. Water — like a squeezed cloth
4. Air — sticks and turning
5. 1 m × 1 m × 1 m
6. Warm stick = working
items.layout:
Headline; heap 55% left + four need icons stacked right; bottom strip 20%; small
"never in the heap" row of crossed icons (bone, bottle, tin, oil, plastic bag).
items.teach_it:
1. Energiser: Compost Heap (green sit, brown stand, water wave, air jump).
2. Point the four needs; brown 2–3 : green 1.
3. GROUPS: build (30 min) — sticks, then brown / green / manure / soil / water, repeat.
4. Squeeze test; stick in the middle; cover.
5. Turn after a week; ready in 2–3 months.
KEY: Green + brown + water + air = compost.

items.title: Liquid manure & worm farm
items.headline: Plant food you can pour
items.labels:
1. Manure in a sack
2. 2 weeks, stir
3. 1 cup + 10 cups water
4. On the soil
5. Red compost worms
6. Shade, damp, no citrus
items.layout: Headline; two equal halves separated by a Hairline rule.
items.teach_it:
1. Liquid manure: each group does one step (sack, hang, fill, lid, who stirs).
2. SAY: 2 weeks; 1 cup to 10 cups water; soil not leaves; every 2 weeks.
3. Worm farm: each group one step (holes, bedding, worms, peels, sack).
4. Rules: shade, damp, no citrus/onion/meat/oil.
KEY: Liquid manure 1 : 10 on the soil. Worms make the best compost.

items.title: Beds that hold water
items.headline: Dig once, feed for years
items.labels:
1. 1 m wide — never step in
2. 50–60 cm deep
3. Layers like a sandwich
4. Subsoil in the middle
5. Mulch on top
6. Keyhole bed
items.layout: Headline; trench cut-away 60%; keyhole 30%.
items.teach_it:
1. Point ①–⑤: 1 m wide, deep, layers, topsoil on top, mulch.
2. GROUPS: peg 1 m × 2 m; dig — topsoil one side, subsoil the other (rotate every 10 min).
3. Layer: coarse → manure → green → dry → soil → water; repeat.
4. Top 15 cm: topsoil + compost; lip at the edges; mulch; water.
5. Hard ground? Build a no-dig raised bed on cardboard.
KEY: Deep layered beds hold water and food for years. 1 m wide, never step on it.

items.title: Grow strong seedlings
items.headline: A strong start
items.labels:
1. Sow straight / sow in trays
2. 1 compost : 1 sand : 1 soil
3. Twice as deep as the seed
4. Damp, light shade
5. Harden off 1 week
6. Plant out at 4–6 leaves
items.layout: Three columns; headline across the top.
items.teach_it:
1. Sort crops: straight in the bed vs seedlings first.
2. GROUPS: sieve and mix 1:1:1.
3. Every learner fills and sows their own tray (2 seeds per hole).
4. Label, water, shade.
5. Care: morning water; harden off; transplant late afternoon.
KEY: Twice as deep as the seed. Harden off, then transplant.

items.title: Planting plan: spacing & rotation
items.headline: The right place, the right distance
items.labels:
1. 10 cm · onion, beetroot
2. 30 cm · spinach, lettuce
3. 45 cm · cabbage, tomato
4. Triangle pattern
5. Beans → Leaves → Fruits → Roots
items.layout:
Headline; bed plan 55% with a spacing table box (the four rows from day-4.md);
rotation wheel 40%.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: too close? too far?
2. GROUPS: make a spacing stick (notches every 10 cm; 15, 30, 45 marked).
3. Plan the bed on paper: 3+ crops; facilitator checks.
4. Mark with the stick, transplant, sow, water, mulch.
5. Rotation: four learners walk the wheel.
KEY: Plan on paper, use the stick, mix crops, rotate every season.

items.title: Healthy garden, fewer pests
items.headline: Climb the ladder from the bottom
items.labels:
1. Healthy soil
2. Many plants
3. Look twice a week
4. Hands and barriers
5. Invite friends
6. Home-made spray
7. Bought poison — last
items.layout:
Headline; ladder 80% with labels on the left of each rung and scenes on the right;
recipe box at the bottom-right: garlic + chilli + onion + water + soap; 1 cup : 4 cups.
items.teach_it:
1. Bug hunt: one pest and one friend per group (15 min).
2. Climb the ladder bottom to top. ASK: where do most people start?
3. GROUPS: make the spray; label it; gloves; wash hands.
4. Collars round seedlings; a board for slugs.
KEY: Start at the bottom. Every pest has an enemy — invite the friends.

items.title: Food-forest layers & planting a fruit tree
items.headline: Plant like a forest
items.labels:
1. Tall tree · small tree · bush
2. Herbs · ground cover · roots · climber
3. 60 × 60 × 60 cm
4. Same depth as the bag
5. Basin, stake, mulch
items.layout: Headline; forest 55%; 6-step strip 40%.
items.teach_it:
1. Name the seven layers; ASK who waters the forest.
2. GROUPS: each group one planting step (pit, mix, depth, plant, basin + stake, water + mulch).
3. SAY: best at the start of the rains; water weekly in the first dry season.
KEY: Layers look after each other. Same depth, basin, mulch.

items.title: Save your seed
items.headline: Seed is life — keep it
items.labels:
1. Open-pollinated — save it
2. Hybrid (F1) — don't
3. Dry method
4. Wet method
5. Cool, dark, dry, labelled
6. 8 of 10 sprout = good
items.layout: Headline; three horizontal bands.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: where did your grandmother get seed?
2. Open-pollinated vs F1; treated seed is poison.
3. Choose the best, from many plants.
4. GROUPS: dry method (beans) and wet method (tomato); show the 2-day ferment.
5. Store: jar, ash, label. Test 10 seeds.
6. Seed swap: take 5, bring back double.
KEY: Save from the best, from many. Cool, dark, dry, labelled.

items.title: Eat the rainbow
items.headline: The garden on the plate
items.labels:
1. Half: vegetables & fruit
2. Quarter: pap, bread, potato
3. Quarter: beans, eggs, fish, meat
4. Dark green every day
5. Orange for eyes & health
items.layout:
Headline; plate 55%; family around it; colour icons strip; question strip:
*"Which colour is missing in your home?"*
items.teach_it:
1. Point the plate: half, quarter, quarter.
2. The colours: green (iron), orange (vitamin A), beans (growing), red/purple and fruit.
3. GROUPS: plate game with 16 food cards (3 plates for a family with a small child).
4. GROUPS: summer and winter crops for each colour.
5. Harvest, weigh, record: eaten / shared / sold.
KEY: Half the plate vegetables and fruit; dark green and orange every day.

items.title: Money in, money out
items.headline: The garden has its own pocket
items.labels:
1. House · Garden · Savings
2. Money in
3. Money out
4. Write it the same day
5. Cost per bunch first
items.layout: Headline; tins 35%; book 35%; price sum 20%.
items.teach_it:
1. Two pockets: house money, garden money.
2. GROUPS: market-day cards with play money and 3 tins.
3. Everyone writes the lines on the money page; add up.
4. Worked price: R100 ÷ 40 bunches = R2.50 each; compare the spaza price.
KEY: Garden money has its own pocket. Write every rand, the same day.

items.title: My 90-day garden plan
items.headline: My next 90 days
items.labels:
1. First 2 weeks
2. By 6 weeks
3. By 90 days
4. My buddy
items.layout:
Headline; path art 60% with writing boxes; an A4 version is the learner's plan
sheet.
items.teach_it:
1. Read the example plan (day-5.md S4).
2. Everyone fills 2–3 actions per stone (drawing fine).
3. 2 minutes each to the group; two stars and a wish.
4. Choose a buddy; write the name.
KEY: Small steps, written down, checked by a buddy.

items.title: The three families
items.brief:
Three side-by-side scenes, equal width, one per family, same style, a thin Hairline
divider between them. **Left — the Dlamini household (rural KZN):** a rondavel and a small
block house on a green hillside; a 2 500 ℓ plastic water tank beside the house; trench beds with
leafy greens, cabbages and a row of maize. A grandmother (70s, headscarf, cardigan) seated on a
chair; her daughter (40s) standing with a hoe; a young man (early 20s) with a phone in his
pocket; two children (8 and 12) carrying a watering can. **Middle — the Mokoena household
(peri-urban Free State):** a small RDP-style house with a fence of droppers and wire, flat dry
grassland beyond; three raised beds with greens and onions, a small plot of green maize. A woman
(mid-30s, braids) tying a bunch of greens; a boy (11) and a girl (6) at her side. **Right —
Sizanani Youth Garden (Mpumalanga):** a church building with a corrugated-iron roof; beside it a
plot with seedling trays on a bench under shade-cloth and greens in rows; three young people
(two men, one woman, 21–27) carrying buckets of water. Sun high in the north (shadows fall to the
south). No text.

items.title: Play money artwork
used_in: R-D2-04 (and printed for the kit — resources.md §3)
items.brief:
Artwork for printed **play money** notes and coins. Notes 120 × 60 mm (clearly smaller
than real notes, which must not be copied), coins 30 mm circles. Each note: Paper background,
a big plain oval on the left with a simple **crop** drawing (R10 = a bean pod, R20 = a spinach
leaf, R50 = a cabbage, R100 = a maize cob), a thick colour band down the right side (R10 Leaf,
R20 Ochre, R50 Ink with a dotted pattern, R100 Forest — Water blue is kept for water only), and an empty
box top right where the **value is typeset** large ("R10") with the words "PLAY MONEY — NOT
LEGAL TENDER" typeset along the bottom by the layout (not in the art). Coins: R1, R2, R5 as plain
circles with a seed pattern, colour Ochre / Mid-green / Ink outline. Deliver as layered
SVG/PDF so values are typeset text. **Must not resemble any real SA banknote.**

items.brief:

Middle ground: a hawker's wheelbarrow stall with greens and tomatoes; a spaza shop with a serving
hatch and crates (no signage). Background: minibus taxis (no branding), people of all ages.
Generic notes changing hands at the hawker stall. No text.

trusted. No text.

items.title: Our money agreement
items.headline: Our money agreement
items.labels:
1. Made-up families only
2. You may pass
3. It stays here
4. No selling here
5. Every question counts
Question: *What else do we agree?*
items.layout:
Headline top band; art 60% with five callouts round the circle; labels in two rows;
blank space at the bottom (5 cm) for learners' signatures or marks — or a sheet beside it.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P01  Our money agreement                     (≈ 12 min)
1. ASK: When you hear "money", what do you feel? One word each.
2. POINT ①: We use made-up families. Nobody shares their own money.
3. POINT ②: You may say "pass". Nobody asks why.
4. POINT ③: What is said here stays here.
5. POINT ④: Nobody sells anything in this room — not us, not visitors.
6. POINT ⑤: Every question is a good question.
7. ASK: What else must we agree? Add 3. Everyone signs or marks.
KEY: Money is private. Here we learn with made-up families.
```

items.title: The money map
items.headline: Where does money go?
items.labels:
1. Money comes in
2. Our household
3. Money goes out
4. Small leaks add up
Question: *Which is your biggest leak?*
items.layout:
Landscape-style art on a portrait sheet: in-arrows left, out-arrows right; labels
under each side; ④ callout at the drips.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P02  The money map                    (≈ 10 min + 30 min practical)
1. DO: Pour water into a bottle with holes. ASK: Where does it go?
2. POINT ①: Money comes in — grant, wages, piece jobs, garden sales.
3. POINT ②: The household in the middle.
4. POINT ③: Money goes out — food is the biggest arrow.
5. POINT ④: Small leaks add up — airtime, sweets, cold drinks.
6. GROUPS: Build your family's map with beans. 1 bean = R50.
7. ASK: Which pile is biggest? What is left at the end?
KEY: See it before you fix it.
```

items.title: Needs first, wants later
items.headline: Needs first, wants later
items.labels:
1. Need: must have
2. Want: can wait
3. It depends
Question: *When is airtime a need?*
items.layout: Scale centred; labels under each basket; ③ in the middle.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P03  Needs first, wants later                (≈ 5 min + 15 min sort)
1. ASK: What can a family NOT live without?
2. POINT ①: Needs — food, water, school, clinic, soap.
3. POINT ②: Wants — nice, but can wait.
4. POINT ③: It depends — airtime to call the clinic is a need; for games, a want.
5. GROUPS: Sort 24 cards into Need / Want / It depends.
6. DO: Give each group a shock card. What will they cut? Wants first.
KEY: When money is short, cut wants before needs. Each family decides.
```

items.title: Plan the month before it starts
items.headline: Plan the month first
items.labels:
1. Count money in
2. Needs first
3. Save some
4. Farm money aside
5. Then wants
6. Keep for surprises
Question: *What did you forget last month?*
items.layout:
Art centred; the six labels line up with the six rows (left of the sheet); question
at the bottom.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P04  Plan the month first                     (≈ 7 min + 20 min practical)
1. ASK: Before a long journey, what do you do? (plan, save the fare)
2. SAY: A budget is a plan for the month, made BEFORE it starts.
3. POINT ①→⑥ in order: in · needs · save · farm · wants · surprises.
4. GROUPS: Collect your family's month in play money. Put notes on each row, in order.
5. RULE: keep at least R100 for surprises.
6. ASK: What did you cut to keep R100?
KEY: Plan before the month starts. Needs, save, farm — then wants.
```

items.title: Three tins
items.headline: Three tins
items.labels:
1. Home
2. Save
3. Farm
4. Garden money in first
Question: *Who decides the split?*
items.layout: Tins across the middle; labels directly under each tin; ④ callout at the hand.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P05  Three tins                        (≈ 5 min + 10 min practical)
1. TELL: Lerato's R120 went in her purse. By Friday it was gone. No money for seed.
2. ASK: What went wrong? (garden money mixed with home money)
3. POINT ③ ④: Every garden rand goes into FARM first — and into the book.
4. POINT ① ②: Once a week the family decides: some stays FARM, some to SAVE, some HOME.
5. GROUPS: Label three tins. Split R300 of play money. Explain why.
6. ASK: Who should decide? The people who work for it should have a say.
KEY: The farm pays the home — on purpose, not by accident.
```

items.title: Ways to save
items.headline: Ways to save
items.labels:
1. Savings group
2. Bank account
3. Money on phone
4. Tin at home
Question: *Which two will you use?*
items.layout: 2 × 2 grid; label under each panel.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P06  Ways to save                      (≈ 5 min + 15 min scoring)
1. ASK: Where did your grandmother keep money? Honour the answers.
2. POINT ①: Savings group / stokvel: save together, small loans, share-out. Three locks, three keys.
3. POINT ②: Bank or Postbank account: safe; fees; grants can be paid in.
4. POINT ③: Money on the phone: quick; fees; lost phone = risk.
5. POINT ④: Tin at home: quick and free; easy to spend or steal.
6. GROUPS: For each way, a bean for each YES: safe? quick? free? helps me keep saving?
7. SAY: Bank money is protected by law up to R100 000. A stokvel is not — keep records.
KEY: Save somewhere safe AND somewhere quick — often two places.
```

items.title: Keep your money safe
items.headline: Keep your money safe
items.labels:
1. PIN: tell nobody
2. Cover the keypad
3. Never share OTP
4. Too good? Scam!
5. Nobody keeps your card
Question: *Who asked for your PIN?*
items.layout:
Shield centre (can hold the SASSA toll-free number in the translated version —
number only, not counted as words); five scenes round it with callouts.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P07  Keep your money safe               (≈ 5 min + 15 min game)
1. POINT ①: Your PIN is yours only — not SASSA, not the bank, not family.
2. POINT ②: Cover the keypad. No "help" from strangers at the ATM.
3. POINT ③: The bank SMS number (OTP) is never for a caller.
4. POINT ④: Big prize, big return? It's a hook.
5. POINT ⑤: No shop, lender or relative may keep your card.
6. GAME: Scam or safe? Read 10 cards; groups show red or green.
7. SAY: Money taken? Phone the number on the back of your card NOW. Grant problems: SASSA 0800 60 10 11.
KEY: Nobody real will ever ask for your PIN or OTP.
```

items.title: The money book
items.headline: Write every rand
items.labels:
1. Date
2. What happened
3. Money in
4. Money out
5. Balance
6. Owed to me
Question: *Does the tin match the book?*
items.layout: Book fills the art area; labels as callouts above each column; ⑥ on the right page.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P08  Write every rand                   (≈ 7 min + 20 min practical)
1. ASK: Lerato's tin has R315. Did she make money? (We can't tell.)
2. POINT ①–⑤: date · what · in · out · balance. One line for every rand, the same day.
3. POINT ⑥: Sold but not paid? Owed to me page — not money in yet.
4. GROUPS: Lerato's week — 10 cards. Move play money, write each line.
5. ASK: Count the tin. Does it match? If not, find the line.
6. ASK: Sold R590. Cash R390. Where is R200? (owed)
KEY: A sale is not cash until you are paid. The tin must match the book.
```

items.title: Where did the harvest go?
items.headline: Where did the harvest go?
items.labels:
1. Eaten
2. Shared
3. Sold
4. Lost
5. Eaten = money saved
Question: *What did you eat this week?*
items.layout: Basket centre, four destinations in the corners, ⑤ small near ①.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P09  Where did the harvest go?          (≈ 5 min + 25 min practical)
1. DO: Put a full basket in the middle. ASK: Where does it go?
2. POINT ①–④: eaten · shared · sold · lost. All four must add up to what you picked.
3. GROUPS: Harvest 5 bunches, weigh one, fill the harvest record for your family.
4. ASK: The family ate 8 bunches. At R12 a bunch, what did they save? (R96)
5. POINT ⑤: Food eaten is money not spent. Write its value.
KEY: Record every harvest. Food eaten is money saved.
```

items.title: Count every cost
items.headline: Count every cost
items.labels:
1. Seed
2. Compost and manure
3. Water
4. Transport
5. Bands, bags, tools
6. Your time
Question: *Which cost do people forget?*
items.layout:
Bed centre, six items in a ring; a small legend strip: solid line = cash, dashed
line = free but not free (the legend is a drawn line sample, no words).
items.teach_it:
```
R-P10  Count every cost                   (≈ 5 min + 20 min sort)
1. ASK: What did it cost to grow this bed? List everything.
2. POINT ①–⑤: seed · compost · water · transport · bands and tools.
3. POINT ⑥ and the dashed lines: your time, your manure, rainwater — free but not free.
4. GROUPS: 12 cost cards → cash costs / free but not free. Add the cash costs with play money.
5. CHECK: Lerato's bed = R510 cash + 44 hours of her time.
6. ASK: Why only R30 for a R90 watering can? (lasts 3 seasons)
KEY: Count every cost — including your own time.
```

items.title: One bunch: cost, price, profit
items.headline: One bunch: cost, price, profit
items.labels:
1. All costs
2. ÷ all bunches
3. Cost of one bunch
4. Floor
5. Market
6. Buyer
Question: *Is your price above the floor?*
items.layout: Two bands: the division (top) and the three price checks (bottom).
items.teach_it:
```
R-P11  One bunch: cost, price, profit     (≈ 10 min + 15 min practical)
1. DO: R40 and 10 bunch tokens. Share the money onto the bunches. (R4 each)
2. POINT ①②③: all costs ÷ all bunches = cost of one bunch. Lerato: R510 ÷ 150 = R3.40.
3. POINT ④: Floor — never sell below R3.40.
4. POINT ⑤: Market — what others charge (check locally).
5. POINT ⑥: Buyer — what this buyer values: fresh, delivered, on time.
6. SUMS: Sales R1 080 − costs R510 = R570 profit. Plus food eaten R480.
7. ASK: Her time — 44 h × R30 = R1 320. Does selling pay her time? Be honest.
KEY: Know your cost of one bunch. Price between the floor and what the buyer values.
```

items.title: Break-even with beans
items.headline: Fill the cup first
items.labels:
1. Season costs cup
2. Each bunch: one bean
3. Full cup: break-even
4. Then profit
Question: *How many bunches fill your cup?*
items.layout: Left-to-right flow: bunches → cup → basket.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P12  Fill the cup first (break-even)    (≈ 5 min + 15 min practical)
1. TELL: Sizanani sells to the creche at R12. Each bunch uses R2 of seed, compost, band.
2. ASK: What does each bunch leave? (R10 = 1 bean)
3. POINT ①: Season costs that don't change: fence R200, cans R100, transport R300 = R600 = 60 beans.
4. POINT ②: Each bunch sold drops one bean in the cup.
5. POINT ③: 60 bunches — the cup is full. Break-even.
6. POINT ④: Bunch 61 onwards — profit.
7. TRY: Price falls to R10. Each bunch leaves R8. How many now? (75)
KEY: Fill the cup first. After break-even, each bunch is profit.
```

items.title: Money through the season
items.headline: Money through the season
items.labels:
1. Money out first
2. Money in later
3. Family big months
4. Pinch month
5. Save ahead
Question: *Which month is hardest for you?*
items.layout:
Headline top left; 12 panels across; labels as callouts; the question bottom right.
Month names are **stuck on** by the facilitator in the local language (not part of the word count).
items.teach_it:
```
R-P13  Money through the season           (≈ 5 min + 25 min practical)
1. DO: Stick up local month names, September on the left.
2. POINT ①: Money goes out first — seed, compost, before any harvest.
3. POINT ②: Money comes in later, when you harvest.
4. POINT ③: Family big months — December, January school.
5. POINT ④: The pinch month — the tin is lowest. ASK: Which month is hardest here?
6. GROUPS: Dlamini farm tin, Sep–Feb, with play money. Colour red when below zero.
7. POINT ⑤: Save ahead in good months for the pinch month.
KEY: Money goes out before it comes in. Save ahead for the pinch month.
```

items.title: Who buys? What do they want?
items.headline: Who buys? What do they want?
items.labels:
1. Neighbour
2. Spaza shop
3. Hawker
4. Creche kitchen
5. Market stall
6. Sell together
Question: *Which buyer pays on time?*
items.layout: Hub-and-spoke; labels at the end of each path.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P14  Who buys?                          (≈ 5 min + 15 min practical)
1. DO: Price board — what prices did you see for a bunch? Why different?
2. POINT ①–⑤: neighbour · spaza · hawker · creche · market.
3. GROUPS: Rank the 6 buyer cards for your family. Why? (amount, price, when paid, quality, distance)
4. DO: Good bunch, bad bunch. Which would you buy?
5. POINT ⑥: Sell together — bigger orders, shared taxi. Needs clear records.
KEY: Who you sell to changes your price. Quality is price.
```

items.title: From order to receipt
items.headline: From order to receipt
items.labels:
1. Order
2. Deliver and count
3. Invoice: you owe
4. Paid
5. Receipt: you paid
Question: *Which paper proves payment?*
items.layout: Panels 1–3 in the top row, 4–5 below; big arrow numbers ①–⑤.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P15  From order to receipt              (≈ 8 min + 60 min market day)
1. TELL: The creche says "it was only 20 bunches". What can Lerato show?
2. POINT ①: Order — what, how many, price, when.
3. POINT ②: Deliver — the buyer counts and signs.
4. POINT ③: Invoice — what they owe, by when. Your copy stays in the book.
5. POINT ④⑤: Paid — then a receipt. The buyer keeps the top copy.
6. DEMO 3 minutes, then MARKET DAY: groups buy and sell with role cards.
7. ASK: Who still owes you? Write it on the Owed page. Practise a polite reminder.
KEY: Each paper proves one step. Money owed is not money in the tin.
```

items.title: Borrow wisely
items.headline: Borrow wisely
items.labels:
1. What for?
2. Total cost?
3. Can I pay?
4. Registered lender?
5. What if?
6. Nobody keeps your card
Question: *Is it cheaper to save first?*
items.layout:
Crossroads centre; labels as a numbered list on the right (they are the five
questions + the rule), callouts link to the art.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P16  Borrow wisely                      (≈ 10 min + 20 min practical)
1. TELL: Bongani wants a R3 000 pump now. Where can he get it?
2. POINT ①–⑤: What for? Total cost? Can I pay? Registered? What if?
3. GROUPS: 4 offer cards. Count with play money: gets · pays back · cost.
   (A R1 500 · B R840 · C R450 · D R0). Can the garden pay each month?
4. POINT ⑥: Keeps your ID or card, asks your PIN? Against the law. Walk away.
5. SAY: Check a lender: NCR 0860 627 627. Too much debt: a registered debt counsellor.
6. RULES: Never borrow with interest for food or parties. Borrow less, for less time.
7. The reserve tin: R20 a week → R500 in 25 weeks.
KEY: Compare the total cost, not the monthly payment.
```

items.title: My money plan
items.headline: My money plan
items.labels:
1. My goal
2. My three tins
3. My book, my day
4. Pinch month, reserve
5. One step next month
Question: *What is your one step?*
items.layout: People at the bottom; five pictures in an arc above; labels with each picture.
items.teach_it:
```
R-P17  My money plan                      (≈ 3 min + 25 min planning & sharing)
1. POINT ①–⑤: goal · three tins · book day · pinch month & reserve · one step.
2. SAY: Your plan is yours. Pictures and ticks are fine. No real amounts needed.
3. DO: 15 minutes — everyone makes their own plan.
4. GROUPS: 2 minutes each: my goal and my one step. The group gives one star.
KEY: One step next month is better than ten steps never.
```

items.title: Two ways to listen
items.brief:
0–7 s: the farmer talks with open hands; the mentor stands, looks at her phone, glances
at her watch; the farmer's gestures slow and stop, shoulders drop. 7–8 s: soft wipe. 8–15 s:
same farmer; the mentor puts the phone in her bag, squats to his level, nods; the farmer
straightens, gestures more, points to a bed. 15–16 s: hold, loop.

items.title: Walk beside
items.headline: Walk beside, not in front
items.labels:
1. In front: I lead
2. Behind: I push
3. Beside: we walk
items.layout: Headline top band; three scenes in the art area with ①②③; label strip below.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: Who was the best helper you ever had? What did they do?
2. POINT ①: the helper in front — when is that right? (new skill, danger)
3. POINT ②: behind — how does a farmer feel when pushed?
4. POINT ③: beside — the farmer chooses the path; the mentor walks with them.
5. GROUPS: sort your helper stories under ① ② ③.
KEY: Walk beside. The farmer chooses the path.

items.title: The mentor's promise
items.headline: The mentor's promise
items.labels:
1. I listen first
2. Only real promises
3. Your story stays private
4. No gifts that bind
5. I keep you safe
items.layout: Hand centred; five callouts on the fingers; labels in a list below.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: What happens when a mentor promises a tank and none comes?
2. POINT ①–⑤ one by one; ask for one example of each.
3. GROUPS: one "What would you do?" card each (day-1.md S1).
4. SAY: Tea is hospitality. A chicken is a gift that binds.
5. SAY: Harm to a child or adult — tell your supervisor the same day.
KEY: Promise only what you can do.

items.title: Listen with ears, eyes and heart
items.headline: Listen with ears, eyes, heart
items.labels:
1. Ears: let them finish
2. Eyes: same level
3. Heart: notice feelings
4. Say it back
items.layout: Scene centre; four callouts; labels below.
items.teach_it:
1. PAIRS: 1 minute of bad listening. How did it feel?
2. POINT ①: count to 3 before you speak.
3. POINT ②: sit or squat at their level; phone away.
4. POINT ③: "You sound tired of this."
5. POINT ④: "So the water runs out in week two…"
6. TRIADS: speaker · listener · observer, 3 rounds.
KEY: Say it back, then ask. No advice yet.

items.title: The question ladder
items.headline: Climb the question ladder
items.labels:
1. Closed: yes or no
2. Open: how, what
3. Deeper: what happens
4. Their plan: what else?
items.layout: Ladder runs bottom-left to top-right; callouts on rungs; labels beside each rung.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: "Did you water?" — what answer do you get? (yes)
2. POINT ②: "How do you water the beds?"
3. POINT ③: "What happens to the water after you pour it?"
4. POINT ④: "What could you try? What else?"
5. GROUPS: climb 10 closed-question cards.
6. SAY: Start with "What are you proud of?"
KEY: The best answer is the one the farmer finds.

items.title: I do · We do · You do
items.headline: I do · We do · You do
items.labels:
1. I do: show once
2. We do: together
3. You do: watch quietly
4. Talk: what worked?
items.layout: Four panels in a Z order; callouts ①–④; labels below each panel.
items.teach_it:
1. DO: explain the A-frame by talking only. Ask a volunteer to build it. Why was it hard?
2. POINT ①: show once, slowly, say each step.
3. POINT ②: the farmer's hands, your help.
4. POINT ③: hands in pockets. Say nothing.
5. POINT ④: What went well? What was hard?
6. Result: demonstrated alone = Demonstrated. Anything else = Needs further support.
KEY: One skill per visit. The farmer's hands.

items.title: The action agreement
items.headline: One action, one owner, one date
items.labels:
1. What?
2. Who?
3. By when?
4. How will we know?
items.layout: Handshake centre; the four vignettes in the corners with ①–④.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: "I'll try to mulch" vs "I will mulch the 2 front beds by Friday" — which happens?
2. POINT ①: one small action, the farmer's words.
3. POINT ②: a named person.
4. POINT ③: before the next contact.
5. POINT ④: what we will see.
6. GROUPS: fix "Farmer must improve the soil".
KEY: What · Who · By when · How we'll know.

zu.headline: Umsebenzi owodwa, umuntu oyedwa, usuku olulodwa

items.title: The Visit Hand
items.headline: Five fingers, five steps
items.labels:
1. Look back
2. Walk and look
3. Listen and ask
4. Try it together
5. Agree and record
items.layout: Hand fills art area; labels curve beside each finger with ①–⑤.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: hold up your hand — what are the 5 steps of a visit?
2. POINT ①: "Last time you planned… show me." (5–10 min)
3. POINT ②: "What are you proud of?" Farmer leads. (15 min)
4. POINT ③: "What would help most right now?" (10 min)
5. POINT ④: one skill, I do · We do · You do. (15 min)
6. POINT ⑤: what · who · by when · how we'll know. Write it at the farm. (10 min)
KEY: Never cut the ring or little finger.

items.title: What to look at, stage by stage
items.headline: What to look at, stage by stage
items.labels:
1. Baseline
2. Planting and spacing
3. Growth and pests
4. Harvest and weigh
5. Selling surplus
6. Review and seed
items.layout: Six equal panels in a row; callouts ①–⑥; labels below.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: Where are most of your gardens today? Point.
2. POINT ②: the spacing string — check one row on every establishment visit.
3. POINT ④: weigh, don't count bunches.
4. SAY: Pick 3–5 checks for the stage and the farmer's priority (playbook §5).
5. SAY: ★ = a Course 1 skill — look for it.
KEY: Look at what matters for this stage.

items.title: Traffic light: who needs me most?
items.headline: Who needs me most?
items.labels:
1. Red: every 2 weeks
2. Amber: every month
3. Green: cluster plus phone
items.layout: Traffic light left third; scenes and labels right; ①②③.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: 40 farmers, 20 working days — can you see all every week?
2. POINT ①: not started, crisis, missed 2 contacts, asked for help.
3. POINT ②: growing, needs further support.
4. POINT ③: skills demonstrated, could host.
5. SAY: Re-sort every month. The colour is private.
6. GROUPS: sort the 40 case cards.
KEY: Nobody goes a month without a contact.

items.title: A mentor's week
items.headline: A mentor's week
items.labels:
1. One cluster a day
2. Cluster visit weekly
3. Farthest first
4. Friday: phone, records
items.layout: Map top 55%; weekday strip below; callouts ①–④.
items.teach_it:
1. DO the sum: Red × 2 + Amber = visits needed.
2. POINT ①: each weekday belongs to one cluster — less travel.
3. POINT ②: the cluster visit rotates A → B → C → D.
4. POINT ③: start far, work back towards home.
5. POINT ④: phones, records, planning, buddy.
6. GROUPS: draw your week on the A3 grid.
KEY: Plan by cluster and route, and leave spare time.

items.title: The cluster visit
items.headline: Learn in a neighbour's garden
items.labels:
1. Welcome and register
2. Host's tour
3. Try it together
4. Share circle
5. Everyone agrees one action
items.layout: Scene with ①–⑤ in visit order; labels below.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: How many farmers can you reach in 2½ hours this way? (8–12)
2. POINT ①: register, consent, last month's actions.
3. POINT ②: the host shows what works; ask the host open questions.
4. POINT ③: 2–3 stations, groups of 3–4.
5. POINT ④: farmers answer each other first.
6. POINT ⑤: one action each, aloud; next host.
KEY: The host teaches; the mentor asks. Rotate the host.

items.title: Phone check-in
items.headline: Ten minutes on the phone
items.labels:
1. Greet
2. Look back
3. Show me
4. What's next?
5. Date
items.layout: Two halves; five numbered steps down the centre line.
items.teach_it:
1. PAIRS: sit back to back — like a phone.
2. POINT ①: "How are you and the family?"
3. POINT ②: "Last time you planned… how did it go?"
4. POINT ③: "Can you send a photo — or describe it?"
5. POINT ④–⑤: "What will you do this week? I'll call on…"
6. SAY: Write it — phone log or Record visit.
KEY: Green farmers stay connected with 10 minutes a month.

items.title: The season journey
items.headline: Six months with our farmers
items.labels:
1. Baseline
2. Establish
3. Grow
4. Harvest
5. Sell
6. Review
items.layout:
Path across the full width; ①–⑥ at stops; a legend row for the contact symbols
(symbols only, words typeset: visit · cluster · phone · field day).
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: What happens in a garden over six months?
2. POINT ①–⑥: one sentence per stop (playbook §7).
3. POINT the symbols: which contact fits which farmer?
4. SAY: Field days at first harvest and at the review.
5. GROUPS: put your cluster visits on the path.
KEY: Every month, every farmer, one contact at least.

items.title: Two tracks, same records
items.headline: Phone or paper: same records
items.labels:
1. Weigh and record
2. Money in, out
3. Keep the slip
4. Invoice the buyer
5. Read the season
items.layout: Two lanes top to bottom; callouts ①–⑤ on the shared objects.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: She sold spinach for a month. Did she make money? How would she know?
2. POINT the lanes: app or paper — same outcome.
3. POINT ①: weigh first, then write kilograms.
4. POINT ②–③: every rand in and out; every cost has a slip.
5. POINT ④: an invoice is not a payment.
6. POINT ⑤: the month-end summary or the report.
KEY: Paper is never second best.

items.title: When it gets hard
items.headline: When it gets hard
items.labels:
1. Stay calm
2. Listen
3. What can they do?
4. Who else can help?
items.layout: Footprints ①–④ across the art; labels below.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: What hard things happen to our farmers? (drought, theft, conflict, drop-out, waiting for inputs)
2. POINT ①: breathe, sit down.
3. POINT ②: say back, no blame.
4. POINT ③: their options, their choice — start small.
5. POINT ④: neighbours, the group, programme, clinic, SAPS, helplines.
6. SAY: Danger now: SAPS 10111 · Childline 116 · GBV 0800 428 428.
KEY: You are a mentor, not a rescuer. Refer and record.

items.title: Show me what changed
items.headline: Show me what changed
items.labels:
1. Before
2. After
3. The date
4. What we saw
items.layout: Before/after top two-thirds; notebook scene below; ①–④.
items.teach_it:
1. ASK: How would a funder know this garden changed?
2. POINT ①②: same spot, same angle — mark the spot at the first visit.
3. POINT ③④: close an action with a date and evidence.
4. SAY: Not done is information: "What got in the way?"
5. GROUPS: which photo pair proves the action?
KEY: An action is closed only with a date and evidence.

ABSOLUTELY NO WORDS OR LETTERS anywhere — sticky notes and flipcharts are blank or show only
icons and scribble-lines.

Landscape 16:9 composition.

Subject: A busy practical site with eight hazards for learners to find: a spade lying point-up on a path; a garden fork leaning at head height; an open spray bottle next to a plate of food; a hosepipe across a walkway; a group working in full midday sun with no hats; a first aid box inside a closed car; someone swinging a pick with a person standing just behind; no water container anywhere. Everything else looks normal and friendly — no injuries shown.

items.title: Our learning agreement
items.headline: Our learning agreement
items.labels:
1. We made it
2. We keep it
Question: *What helps you learn?*
items.layout:
Headline band; art in the top 45%; labels ① ② as two small ochre tags at the left of
the ruled area; ruled writing area 50%; question strip at the bottom.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P01  Our learning agreement                     (≈ 15 min)
1. ASK: What would help you learn this week? One idea per sticky note.
2. DO: Groups agree 3; Reporters stick them on the lines.
3. DO: Cluster and read back. Add missing must-haves (phones, time,
   right to pass, no correcting language, feedback = thank you,
   Question Tree).
4. DO: Everyone signs or marks. A thumbprint counts.
5. ASK (every morning): Are we keeping it? What needs to change?
KEY: An agreement made by the group is kept by the group.
```

items.title: How adults learn — the learning cycle
items.headline: How adults learn
items.labels:
1. Do
2. Look back
3. Make sense
4. Use it
Question: *Where do your lessons stop?*
items.layout: Headline top; loop fills 60%; ①–④ ochre circles on each arrow; labels band below.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P02  How adults learn                          (≈ 12 min)
1. DO first: any short hands-on task (fold a seed envelope).
2. POINT ①: What did you do?
3. POINT ②: What did you notice? What went wrong?
4. POINT ③: What is the rule? Why does it work?
5. POINT ④: When will you use it at home?
6. SAY: Adults want the why, bring experience, learn from real
   problems, need respect. Go all the way round.
KEY: Most bad lessons stop at "make sense". Finish with "use it".
```

items.title: Every lesson: Look · Try · Talk · Take home
items.headline: Look · Try · Talk · Take home
items.labels:
1. Hook them
2. Hands on
3. Three questions
4. One action
Question: *Who talks most in each step?*
items.layout:
Headline top; four bands 15% each; ①–④ ochre circles at the left edge of each band;
labels at the right edge of each band; question strip at the bottom.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P03  Look · Try · Talk · Take home             (≈ 10 min)
1. ASK: Think of a lesson you just had. What came first?
2. POINT ①: Look — a question, object, story or poster reveal.
3. POINT ②: Try — every learner's hands, in groups of 5.
4. POINT ③: Talk — What did you do? Why does it work?
   What will you do at home?
5. POINT ④: Take home — each group says one action.
6. ASK: Who talks most in each step? (Learners, except a
   short set-up.)
KEY: Try comes before the long explanation.
```

items.title: The teacher-talk meter
items.headline: Teacher talk: 30% or less
items.labels:
1. Teacher: 3 in 10
2. Learners: 7 in 10
3. One mark a minute
Question: *Who counted today?*
items.layout:
Headline top; gauge 35%; people 25%; ① on the Ochre wedges, ② on the Leaf wedges,
③ on the clipboard; labels band; question strip.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P04  The teacher-talk meter                    (≈ 8 min)
1. ASK: How much of that lesson was the teacher talking? Guess.
2. DO: Read the tally — one mark per minute of talk to the room.
3. SAY: Talk % = marks ÷ minutes × 100. 60-min session = 18 min max.
4. ASK: Where did the talk happen? Where could it be shorter?
5. SAY: Biggest cut: give the task first, explain after the Try.
KEY: Talk is counted, not guessed. ≤ 30%.
```

items.title: Outcomes start with a doing word
items.headline: Start with a doing word
items.labels:
1. A doing word
2. What
3. How well
Question: *Could you see it by lunch?*
items.layout:
Headline top; art 60%; labels band; question strip. A blank flipchart hangs beside
it for the verbs list in local languages.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P05  Start with a doing word                   (≈ 12 min)
1. SHOW two outcomes: "understand compost" vs "build a heap
   1 m wide in green and brown layers".
2. ASK: At lunch, how would you know each one happened?
3. POINT ①②③: doing word · what · how well.
4. SAY the verbs: make, show, find, measure, explain, name,
   choose, draw, plan, record.
5. SAY foggy words to avoid: understand, know, learn about,
   be aware of, appreciate.
6. DO: Fix three foggy outcomes in groups.
KEY: If you can't see it or hear it, it isn't an outcome.
```

items.title: Groups of 5 — five jobs
items.headline: Five people, five jobs
items.labels:
1. Leader
2. Timekeeper
3. Materials
4. Recorder
5. Reporter
Question: *Whose turn tomorrow?*
items.layout: Headline top; art 60% with ①–⑤ on each person; labels band in two rows; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P06  Five people, five jobs                    (≈ 5 min)
1. POINT ①–⑤: Leader keeps everyone doing, not watching ·
   Timekeeper calls "5 minutes left" · Materials collects and counts
   the kit · Recorder draws or writes · Reporter speaks for the group.
2. DO: Each group chooses today's roles in 1 minute.
3. SAY: Roles rotate every morning — everyone does every job.
4. SAY: Recorder can draw. Seated roles are real roles.
KEY: A job for everyone means nobody only watches.
```

items.title: A practical, not a demo
items.headline: Hands on, not a demo
items.labels:
1. Kit per group
2. Demo: 3 minutes
3. Groups of 5
4. Stations apart
5. Hands behind back
6. One kit? Carousel
Question: *Who watched?*
items.layout:
Headline top; art 60% (①② near the crates and facilitator, ③④ on the stations,
⑤ on her hands, ⑥ on an arrow looping between stations); labels in two rows; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P07  Hands on, not a demo                      (≈ 10 min)
1. STORY (1 min): In 2022, practicals became one person digging while
   25 watched — even with kit for four groups in the car.
2. ASK: Why does it happen? Which reasons can we fix?
3. POINT ①–⑥: count kit per group · show 3 min max · groups of 5
   with roles · stations 3 m apart · hands behind your back ·
   one kit = carousel, nobody watches more than 10 min.
4. SAFETY: tools points down; nobody behind a swing; gloves or soap;
   hats and water; first aid kit open; lightning = stop.
5. DO: Plan a carousel for one A-frame and 25 learners.
KEY: If you take the spade, the practical is over.
```

items.title: The question ladder
items.headline: Climb the question ladder
items.labels:
1. Closed
2. Open
3. Deeper
4. Wait 5 seconds
5. Bounce it back
Question: *What do others think?*
items.layout:
Headline top; ladder art 60%, ①–③ at each rung, ④ on the hand, ⑤ on the ball;
labels band; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P08  Climb the question ladder                 (≈ 12 min)
1. ASK three: "Is soil alive?" · "What lives in soil?" ·
   "How could you find out if YOUR soil is alive?"
2. ASK: Which got the best thinking?
3. POINT ①: Closed — one right answer; for checking.
   ②: Open — many answers: what, how, tell me.
   ③: Deeper — why? how do you know? what if? what will you do?
4. POINT ④: Count five fingers silently before you speak again.
5. POINT ⑤: "What do others think?" — never answer your own question.
6. SAY: Not "Any questions?" — "What questions do you have?"
KEY: Climb the ladder, then wait.
```

items.title: A poster that teaches
items.headline: A poster that teaches
items.labels:
1. One idea
2. 25 words, max
3. Short headline
4. Big picture, no words
5. Numbered labels
6. One question
Question: *Readable from 6 m?*
items.layout:
Headline top; art 55% with ①–⑥ pointing at the parts of the drawn poster; labels in
two rows; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P09  A poster that teaches                     (≈ 15 min + studio)
1. SHOW a bad poster at 6 m: "What does it teach?"
2. ASK groups: What's wrong? Each problem becomes a rule.
3. POINT ①–⑥ and match their rules.
4. ADD: sun in the north · people like our farmers · local
   materials · works in black and white · no words inside the
   picture (so it can be translated).
5. DO: Pencil first. Headline, picture, 3 labels, 1 question.
6. DO: The 6-metre check with a partner.
KEY: One idea, few words, a big picture and a question.
```

items.title: Two stars and a wish
items.headline: Two stars and a wish
items.labels:
1. Teacher speaks first
2. Star: specific
3. Star: specific
4. Wish: "next time maybe"
5. Say thank you
Question: *What will you try next?*
items.layout:
Headline top; art 60% (① on the teacher, ②③ on the stars, ④ on the seedling, ⑤ on the
hand on heart); labels band; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P10  Two stars and a wish                      (≈ 5 min to teach; used daily)
1. POINT ①: The teacher speaks first: what went well, what I'd change.
2. POINT ②③: Two stars — specific: "You let them dig before you
   explained." Not "nice".
3. POINT ④: One wish, as a suggestion: "Next time maybe…"
4. POINT ⑤: The teacher only says "Thank you. Next time I will…"
   No defending.
5. RULE: Never correct anyone's language, spelling or accent.
KEY: Feedback is a gift. Say thank you.
```

items.title: Wake the room — energiser menu
used_in: every opening circle and after lunch
items.headline: Wake the room
items.labels:
1. Sun and Shade
2. Compost Heap
3. Web of Life
4. Rain Storm
5. Pass the Clap
6. Seed Swap
Question: *Who leads the next one?*
items.layout: Headline top; 3 × 2 grid 60% with ①–⑥; labels in two rows; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P11  Wake the room                             (5 min each)
1. WHEN: yawning, phones, after lunch — always after lunch.
2. CHOOSE one that teaches (see facilitation-toolkit §6).
3. CHECK: nobody forced to touch or run; elders may sit and call.
4. RUN it for 3–4 minutes. Stop while it's still fun.
5. ASK: What did it teach?
KEY: From Day 2, trainees lead the energisers.
```

items.title: Teach with what you have (tree talk)
items.headline: Teach with what you have
items.labels:
1. Sun behind learners
2. Poster at eye level
3. Circle: all see
4. Your back to wind
5. Stop, then talk
Question: *What could teach?*
items.layout:
Headline top; art 60% with ①–⑤ placed on the sun, the poster, the horseshoe, the wind
lines and the stake; labels in two rows; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P12  Teach with what you have                  (≈ 12 min)
1. DO: Teach outside first; then ask "what made it work?"
2. POINT ①–⑤: sun behind learners · poster at eye level ·
   horseshoe so all see the object · your back to the wind ·
   stop, then talk — never talk while walking.
3. ASK: What could go wrong outside? (noise, rain, moving shade,
   dogs) What's your plan?
4. GROUPS: List 8 free things that teach (box = sun & shade,
   bottles = runoff, jar = soil, beans = money, string = spacing).
KEY: The best teaching aid is usually already in the yard.
```

items.title: One lesson, three ways
items.headline: One lesson, three ways
items.labels:
1. Poster
2. Slides
3. App
4. Paper backup
Question: *What if the power fails?*
items.layout:
Headline top; columns 60% (①②③ at the top of each, ④ on the paper row); labels band;
question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P13  One lesson, three ways                    (≈ 8 min per mode)
1. POINT ①: Poster — default. Cover and reveal; point and ask;
   learners come to the poster; stand to the side.
2. POINT ②: Slides — test from the back in daylight; TV beats a
   projector; press B to blank; tablet per group of 5 for clips.
3. POINT ③: App — My Studies (lessons offline) · Mentor → Training
   (register, signatures, photos, feedback) · Lima Vision (ask the
   group "do we agree?").
4. POINT ④: Every mode has a paper twin: flip-book, printed stills,
   paper register.
5. ASK: What can a device show that a poster can't? (Movement.)
KEY: Slides and app are a bonus. Switch in 30 seconds.
```

items.title: Hand over, don't take over
items.headline: Hand over, don't take over
items.labels:
1. Plan who leads
2. Say the handover
3. Partner works, quietly
4. Touch ear: offer
5. Star each other
Question: *Who leads next?*
items.layout:
Headline top; art 60% (① on a lesson-plan sheet in a hand, ② on the tray, ③ on the
clipboard, ④ on the inset, ⑤ on the smiles); labels; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P14  Hand over, don't take over                (≈ 6 min)
1. POINT ①: Write who leads Look, Try, Talk, Take home.
2. POINT ②: Hand over out loud: "Now Thandi will show you the jar."
3. POINT ③: The one not leading counts talk, hands out kit, watches
   groups. No side-talk.
4. POINT ④: Agreed signal = "may I add?" The leader says yes or no.
5. POINT ⑤: Debrief together every evening: star each other first.
KEY: Two teachers, one lesson — never two lessons at once.
```

items.title: Did they learn it?
items.headline: Did they learn it?
items.labels:
1. Watch them do it
2. Picture quiz
3. Ask them
Question: *What can they do now?*
items.layout: Headline top; three bands 20% each with ①–③; labels band; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P15  Did they learn it?                        (≈ 10 min)
1. POINT ①: Skills checklist — tick = alone · half = with help ·
   cross = not yet.
   Tick while they work, not from memory.
2. POINT ②: Picture quiz, Day 1 and Day 5 — walk to corners;
   count class totals, not names.
3. POINT ③: Evaluation — fingers 1–5; stickers on "understand best"
   and "want more". The gap = the mentor visit plan.
4. SAY: It records what they can DO. It's not a qualification.
KEY: The best proof is a farmer doing the skill.
```

items.title: Ready by Day 0 — the course kit
items.headline: Ready by Day 0
items.labels:
1. Crates per group
2. Posters up
3. Flip folder
4. First aid open
5. Devices charged
Question: *What's missing?*
items.layout: Headline top; flat-lay 60% with ①–⑤; labels band; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P16  Ready by Day 0                            (≈ 15 min)
1. POINT ①: One crate per group + 1 spare set. Materials counts in/out.
2. POINT ②: Posters up before the session, left to right, seated
   eye level; they stay up all course.
3. POINT ③: Flip folder: register, POPIA, session sheets, checklist,
   quiz, evaluation, daily report, certificates (registered + 10%).
4. POINT ④: First aid kit open; clinic route written down.
5. POINT ⑤: Devices charged; lessons saved offline; tested in
   flight mode.
6. ASK: What's missing? Fix it today.
KEY: Day 0 is never the same day as Day 1.
```

items.title: Everyone learns
items.headline: Everyone learns
items.labels:
1. Pictures, not only words
2. Language time
3. A role for everyone
4. Seated jobs
5. Ask the elders
Question: *Who isn't taking part?*
items.layout: Headline top; art 60% with ①–⑤; labels in two rows; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P17  Everyone learns                           (≈ 15 min)
1. POINT ①: Assume some don't read. Draw, point, do. Recorders draw.
2. POINT ②: After you explain, groups retell it in their own
   language for 2 minutes.
3. POINT ③: Every person has a role; rotate daily.
4. POINT ④: Every practical has a seated job.
5. POINT ⑤: "How did your grandmother do this?" Honour it,
   then add what's new.
6. NEVER ask someone to read aloud unless they volunteer.
KEY: Small changes, planned ahead, and a role for everyone.
```

items.title: Keep the teacher strong
items.headline: Keep the teacher strong
items.labels:
1. Three, then rest
2. Day 0 always
3. Save your voice
4. Hat, water, shade
5. Evening buddy
6. Listen, then refer
Question: *What drains you?*
items.layout: Headline top; ring of scenes 60% with ①–⑥; labels in two rows; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P18  Keep the teacher strong                   (≈ 10 min)
1. POINT ①: Max three courses back to back, then a week at home.
2. POINT ②: Day 0 is a working day. Never skip it.
3. POINT ③: Use the signal, not shouting. Water all day.
4. POINT ④: Heavy work before 11:00; sit while groups work.
5. POINT ⑤: 10 minutes with your co-facilitator every evening.
6. POINT ⑥: Not a counsellor, bank or taxi. Listen, refer, follow up.
7. ASK: What drains you? What will you do about it?
KEY: A tired teacher talks more and listens less.
```

items.title: The 10 elements of agroecology
items.headline: Ten elements of agroecology
items.labels:
1. Diversity
2. Sharing knowledge
3. Synergies
4. Efficiency
5. Recycling
6. Resilience
7. Human values
8. Food culture
9. Fair governance
10. Solidarity economy
Question: *Which is our strongest?*
items.layout: A0 landscape. Headline band; art 65% with ①–⑩; labels in two rows of five; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P19  Ten elements of agroecology               (≈ 20 min with card sort)
1. DO first: groups sort 20 practice photos under the 10 elements.
2. SAY: FAO agreed these 10 in 2018 to describe agroecology.
3. POINT ①–⑩ (FAO names): Diversity · Co-creation & sharing of
   knowledge · Synergies · Efficiency · Recycling · Resilience ·
   Human & social values · Culture & food traditions ·
   Responsible governance · Circular & solidarity economy.
4. ASK: Which 3 is our village strongest in? Which is weakest?
5. SAY: Farming AND the food system — knowledge, culture,
   fair markets, who decides.
KEY: Agroecology is the practice and the food system together.
```

items.title: Twelve design principles
items.headline: 12 design principles
items.labels:
1. Observe
2. Catch energy
3. Get yields
4. Take feedback
5. Use renewables
6. No waste
7. Pattern first
8. Integrate
9. Small, slow
10. Value diversity
11. Use edges
12. Embrace change
items.layout:
A0 landscape. Headline band; clock-face art 70% with ①–⑫; labels as a ring or two
rows of six. (No question line — at 25 words; the question is on the card.)
items.teach_it:
```
T-P20  12 design principles                      (≈ 10 min, trainers' reference)
1. SAY: Permaculture = 3 ethics + a design toolbox. These are
   David Holmgren's widely taught 12.
2. POINT each: 1 Observe & interact · 2 Catch & store energy ·
   3 Obtain a yield · 4 Self-regulate & accept feedback ·
   5 Use & value renewables · 6 Produce no waste · 7 Design from
   patterns to details · 8 Integrate rather than segregate ·
   9 Small & slow solutions · 10 Use & value diversity ·
   11 Use edges & value the margins · 12 Creatively respond to change.
3. ASK: Which one did the "good garden" (F-P03) use?
4. SAY: Course 1 teaches six simpler garden principles (F-P04).
KEY: Ethics say why; principles say how to design.
```

items.title: Test it side by side
items.headline: Test it side by side
items.labels:
1. Two plots, one change
2. Look every week
3. Measure and draw
4. The group decides
Question: *What will you test?*
items.layout: Headline top; art 60% with ①–④; labels band; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P21  Test it side by side                      (≈ 10 min + a season)
1. ASK: How could we find out if compost really helps — ourselves?
2. POINT ①: Two plots (or pots). Change ONE thing only.
3. POINT ②: Same day every week, the group looks together.
4. POINT ③: Measure (a marked stick) and draw what you see.
5. POINT ④: The group decides what worked and what to try next.
6. SAY: This is how farmer field schools learn — by comparing.
KEY: Farmers believe what they see in their own trial.
```

items.title: Calm in a difficult moment
items.headline: Calm in a difficult moment
items.labels:
1. Breathe
2. Name it kindly
3. Listen, ask
4. Offer a way on
5. Follow up privately
Question: *Is everyone safe?*
items.layout: Headline top; art 60% with ①–④ in the main scene and ⑤ on the inset; labels; question.
items.teach_it:
```
T-P22  Calm in a difficult moment                (≈ 25 min with role plays)
1. POINT ①: Slow down. Lower your voice.
2. POINT ②: "I can see you feel strongly about this."
3. POINT ③: "Tell me more." Ask; don't argue.
4. POINT ④: A choice, a role, the Question Tree, a talk at tea.
5. POINT ⑤: Never shame anyone in front of the group.
6. SAFETY: If anyone is at risk, stop and get help. Know the help
   lines (GBV Command Centre 0800 428 428 · check locally).
7. DO: Role plays in threes — facilitator, learner, observer.
KEY: You're not a counsellor. Keep people safe, and refer.
```

man seated close to the facilitator, watching her face as she speaks; two young women talking

items.title: Artwork for T-P19 · The 10 elements of agroecology
items.brief:
A wide, busy but orderly village landscape, read left to right, with
ten clear scenes: (1) a field of maize, beans and pumpkin growing together with a fruit tree;
(2) a woman farmer showing neighbours her trench bed; (3) chickens scratching under fruit trees
beside the garden; (4) a compost heap next to a bed (no bags of fertiliser); (5) kitchen scraps
going into a compost bin; (6) a mulched garden still green beside a dry bare field; (7) youth and
elders planning together around a drawing on the ground; (8) a family eating together from shared
bowls with local greens; (9) a group at a water tank beside a hand-drawn roster board (lines,
not words); (10) a small market stall and a seed-swap table with neighbours. Sun in the north
(upper part of the scene).

Subject: A homestead seen from above in the centre (house, tank, beds, fruit trees, chicken run, swale on the slope), surrounded by twelve small round vignettes like a clock face: (1) a woman sitting watching her yard; (2) a tank full of water and a seed jar; (3) a hand picking spinach; (4) a person checking a flooded bed and redirecting water; (5) the sun and rain falling on a roof; (6) kitchen scraps feeding chickens feeding compost; (7) a view of a whole slope, then a single bed; (8) chickens beside the vegetable garden; (9) one well-made bed; (10) many crops mixed; (11) plants thriving along a fence line; (12) a farmer planting drought-tolerant crops under a hot sky. Thin arrows join each vignette to the part of the homestead it relates to.

items.title: Artwork for T-P21 · Test it side by side
items.brief:
Two small plots side by side, divided by a string line. Left plot:
bare soil, small pale plants. Right plot: mulched soil with compost, taller dark-green plants.
A group of five farmers crouches between them: one measures a plant against a marked stick,
one draws on a clipboard, one holds a handful of soil from each side, two discuss, pointing.
Along the bottom, three small panels show the same two plots getting further apart in growth
over time (week 1, 4, 8 — shown only by plant size, no numbers).

items.title: Artwork for T-P22 · Calm in a difficult moment
items.brief:
Main scene: a facilitator stands relaxed with open palms, shoulders
down, facing a learner who is standing and gesturing angrily; other learners seated watch.
Small inset lower right: the same facilitator and learner seated together on a bench with cups
of tea, talking quietly, the learner calmer. No weapons, no aggression beyond gesture.
